3	# Facts on record
4	
5	## Execution model
6	
7	- Two execution paths share parser and phases and differ at the end: the walk interpreter (`fortress file.fss`) and the bytecode compiler (`fortress compile` + `run`) (`repo-internals.md:95-129`).
8	- The static type checker (Scala, `scala_src/typechecker/`) runs only on the compile path; `walk` turns it off and there is no switch to make it run in the interpreter (`repo-internals.md:127`); every "type error" seen from the interpreter is a run-time dispatch failure.
9	- `fortress typecheck` checks against `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, not the interpreter's prelude, so it is not an oracle for interpreter programs (ledger row 69); making the checker usable on interpreter programs means giving it the interpreter's prelude, which is not a ledger row and not on the worklist as a separate item (it falls under worklist item 2, compiler-path library parity).
10	- The code generator lowers every type to a JVM reference type: `RR64` to the runtime class `FRR64`, no `dadd`/`dmul` anywhere in the generated loop (shown in bytecode, `perf-probes/boxing/javap/`); arrays are library objects over `get`/`put`, not `double[]` (`repo-internals.md:129`).
11	- On microGPT-shaped array code boxing is the dominant representational cost, 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]` in Java models of the program's three kernels, and nothing microGPT-shaped compiles: the compiler prelude lacks the array types, with `Array`, `Vector` and `Array3` undefined in `FlatArrays.fsi` (row 305, wider than row 72). On the interpreter, the only path that runs the kernels, 43.5% is the AST walk, 32.3% environment lookup, 5.2% type dispatch and 0% number representation (JFR on `krows`). The two one-line runtime defects the probe found are fixed (rows 302, 303; the next two entries), and no array type goes into the compiler prelude: the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (POSITIONS, the library route). A failed compile leaves a 0-byte jar in the bytecode cache (`perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md`).
12	- The boxing probe's scalar-loop reading, 156× primitive Java with boxing about 2% of it, is of the tree before rung 0's two fixes (rows 302, 303; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`); of the costs it named, `countedseqloop`'s boxed indices and closure call (about 7%) and the representational rest (about 30%) are unaddressed (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md`).
13	- The eager debug string of `BaseTask.inATransaction()` is fixed: the message is built only under the `debug` flag (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java:248`; row 302; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`).
14	- `FFloatLiteral`'s String round trip is fixed: the literal caches its `double` instead of re-parsing its text in `asRR64()` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FFloatLiteral.java`; row 303; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`).
15	- The benchmark numbers on record from 2026-09-15 (`bench1t` 9.3441 s, `bench1h` 6.0732 s) were taken on a quieter machine: the same unmodified tree measured 13.0566 s and 8.8159 s in another session, so absolute seconds are not comparable across sessions and only a before/after pair taken in one session is (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`).
16	- `ant compileAll` leaves the bytecode cache holding no library jars: the first `fortress compile` after a rebuild of the compiler clears `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/`, and `fortress run` then dies with `NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`; the library-order recompile of `repo-internals.md:170-179` restores it, about two minutes.
17	- The compiled path's bytecode cache can come up empty after a library-order rebuild that reports exit 0; re-running the same commands one at a time produced the jars (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md`).
18	- Generic instantiations are stamped out at class-load time by ASM rewriting of template bytecode (`InstantiatingClassloader.java`, `repo-internals.md:129`); a size is in the stamped class's name (`pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, `perf-probes/nat/java.md` § 1; `reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md`), and its descriptor in a stamped class is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` ("A size is carried at run time as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`" under Landed semantics).
19	- Implicit parallelism: `for` is parallel unless every generator is `seq`; the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator are evaluated in parallel implicit threads (`tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:59`; row 265). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the work-stealing pool; there is no explicit threading in any of our programs.
20	- The compile path's checker cannot check `nat` parameters at all (see "The checker and the one library" below): this no longer holds. The checker checks `nat` and `int` static parameters ("The compiled type checker checks `nat` and `int` static parameters" below), and a sized program loads and runs compiled ("A size is carried at run time as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`" under Landed semantics). Sizes in types (`nat` parameters) are "instantiated at runtime" by the specification (`trait-parameters.tex`, natparams); they check shapes when a value is made or passed; no optimization is built on them anywhere. A `nat`-typed parameter does not unify statically with a run-time-built array (row 23); the interpreter matches at dispatch, and a mismatch reads "Failed to find any matching overload", uncatchable (row 83). A literal size does unify (row 23's positive half).
21	- **The specification's own declaration of `Nothing` compiles on neither path, and the reason is name resolution, not codegen.** The Working Draft's `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/convenience.tex:49`, kept in `Specification/basic-lib/convenience.tex:61-65` marked "Not allowed") stops on both paths with a syntax error at `excludes`, because the grammar gives an object no `excludes` clause (`Specification/basic/objects.tex:84-86`; `reviews/spec-refused-examples/probes/SpecNothing.fss` and its captures). Without that clause, `fortress compile` and `fortress walk` give the identical single error, both rc=255: `T is undefined`, at the `T` inside the extends clause (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-maybe/probes/WhereClauseNothing.fss`, `.txt`; `reviews/spec-refused-examples/probes/SpecNothingNoExcludes.fss`). A where clause on an object declaration does not bind a type variable used in that declaration's extends clause in either implementation. `CodeGen.forObjectDeclPrePass` would refuse the declaration a second time at codegen — `header.getWhereClause().isNone()` is one of its `canCompile` conditions (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:4093`) — but nothing reaches it. 22	- **An exported function fails exactly as an exported variable does when a component's name differs from the api it exports, and the failure is the repository's, not codegen's** (`compile-ladder/rung-export-var/`). # Facts on record

## Execution model

- Two execution paths share parser and phases and differ at the end: the walk interpreter (`fortress file.fss`) and the bytecode compiler (`fortress compile` + `run`) (`repo-internals.md:95-129`).

The table's `#cache` row names the stage's setting and is not an api (`coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh:93-94`). The total is reported and never red on its own, because a fix can raise it and two rungs' changes do not add; the gate stays red on a crash line no rung declared, a stale shadow or a table with no total (`checker_compare`, the gate's step 8), and the post-batch review ties every new or risen row to a named rung edit, reading the landed table (`coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`, "After the landing: the coordinator's routing" and "The checker count, and a rung whose test is that stage").
2	- **The compiled type checker checks `nat` and `int` static parameters** (`compile-ladder/rung-nat-checker/REPORT.md`). A size is a symbol or a literal compared by equality, an unknown one an inference variable of its own (`_InferenceVarInt`, a third constraint track in `Formula`), with `keep-size-params` in `TypeSchemaAnalyzer`, kind-correct static arguments in `AbstractMethodChecker` and `FnNameInfo.boundsFor`, and sizes compared by `ExportChecker.equalIntExprs`. Arithmetic in a size and a `bool`, `dim` or `unit` parameter are refused by name; a size a call leaves unknown is refused at the call (POSITIONS, "Sizes"), stricter than a dead type parameter's `BOTTOM` (`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1937-1940`), and in an overload set as "The compiled checker refuses a call whose most specific arm has a size the call cannot fix" below says. Gated by `compiler_tests/NatInferredChecker`, `NatWrittenChecker`, `NatMethodChecker`, `NatExportChecker` and `XXXNatMismatchChecker`.
3	- **The return-type rule now reads a size as it reads a type parameter** (`compile-ladder/rung-nat-checker/`). `OverloadingOracle.satisfiesReturnTypeRule` keeps a size of the less specific declaration that the domains leave unsolved as that declaration's own parameter, as the paper's `σ∧` binds `Δ2` (`Papers/Types/overloading-check.tick:166-172`), so an override returning `Dn[\T,3,s\]` over `Up[\T,b,s\]` is refused as its type-parameter twin is; `keep-size-params` alone clears the `subarray` refusal, `Formula.imp` unrelaxed (`compile-ladder/rung-nat-checker/probes/typecheck-probes.txt`).
4	- **The checker's return-type rule lets the more specific declaration choose its own instantiation, so an override that permutes its own static parameters in its return type type-checks and fails at run time** does not hold: the checker checks the Return Type Rule over every instance and refuses the permuted override by answer 9's positional rule (row 398, fixed; `compiler_tests/XXXOverloadPermutedStaticParams`; "The compiled checker checks the Return Type Rule over every instance and answer 9's positional rule" below). The cause was the call's written static arguments handed by position to a different arm, not the paper's rule, which accepts the pair (`reviews/overloading-judgement.md` § 8); the specification allows the pair and states the positional rule as the compiled implementation's restriction (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:621-652`). The title's measurement: `compile-ladder/rung-nat-checker/probes/compile-probes.txt:29-33`.
5	- **The compiled checker refuses a call whose most specific arm has a size the call cannot fix** (`compile-ladder/rung-unknown-size-arm/REPORT.md`). `checkApplication` refuses the call, "Could not infer static argument nat n without context", when an arm that failed only on an unknown size is more specific than every candidate and its parameter type is free of that size (`scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala:251`, `:464-473`), at every kind of application; the arm rides in `NoContextError` (`exceptions/ApplicationError.scala:156-164`). Not refused: an arm whose unknown size occurs in its own parameter type, which is dropped (row 400), and a call whose argument's static type lies above the arm's domain, where the compiled run dies reading the size (row 446). A type parameter is bound to `BottomType`, not left unknown, so no type-only arm is refused (row 447). The code generator dies on an overloaded function bound to a variable (row 448). Gated by `compiler_tests/XXXNatUnknownSizeArm`, `XXXNatUnknownSizeVal`, `XXXNatUnknownSizeFnValue`, `NatKnownSizeArm` and `XXXOverloadedFnValue`.
6	- **The written bound `Object` on the three result-only parameters and row 421's four lines take the distance from 1,747 to 1,337 under `any` and from 1,738 to 1,324 under walk's setting; the comprehension's bound clears nothing** (`compile-ladder/rung-result-bounds/`; rows 309, 421, 447, 469-472). ## The territory map

A two-declaration `import java` component in `CompilerBuiltin.fss`'s shape, one `import java` line per helper class from one package, runs on walk under the six patches, +120 −20 lines of Java in six files, one of them new, and prints what the compiled path prints, for top-level functions and for a trait's functional method and an object's dotted method alike; the interpreter suite, what `ant testSystem` runs, is green under them (`testFast` not run). ## The container

- **A boot after a compaction costs about 285K tokens of context, and `FACTS.md` is about two fifths of it** does not hold: a boot costs about 250K of context, and `FACTS.md` is about a third of it (session `fe616d40`'s main transcript, each read's tokens the growth of the next call's prompt). Cost: four workflow agents (~798k tokens), their worktrees, and the 13 hours after the last transcript snapshot; everything pushed was safe, and the batch's record kept the batch runnable. Mechanism, the three traps and the recovery procedure: `explorations/coordinator/remote-container.md`.

Its Stop hook returns at once (0.01 s, where every turn had waited 24-27 s plus the push) and leaves the work to a detached runner, which copies, commits, pushes whenever the branch is ahead of its upstream and packs (`gc --auto` at `gc.auto=1000`), one line per pass in `/home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/.backup.log`, the last 200 kept; a pass takes about 10 s, the copier about 1 s of it. The copier is incremental on size and modification time (`.backup.state`), and its output is byte for byte the old copier's (1,012 files, 958 MB, `diff -r`). Workflow agents' transcripts are among its sources, and a transcript over 64 MiB is split. It swallows every error and never holds up the session, so a failed push shows only in the log's `push=` field. A container that dies within about 10 s of a turn's end loses that turn's snapshot; only an `index.lock` at least 10 s old that no process has open is cleaned, and a stale `/home/user/fortress/.git/refs/heads/transcripts-blinded.lock` fails every later commit (`commit=failed`) until it is removed by hand. Snapshots before the change can be missing: a detached gc inherited the runner's lock and held it while it ran, and every snapshot requested meanwhile was skipped. (`transcripts-blinded@974d9be7`, its message; `coordinator/remote-container.md` § How the snapshot works; the reference copies in `coordinator/transcript-backup/`.) The platform's own Stop hook, `~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh`, comes from the launcher's `--settings /root/.claude/launcher-settings.json` and is rewritten at every process start; it exits 2, which makes the session take another turn, whenever the tree has uncommitted changes, untracked files, or unpushed or unverifiable commits. It is a no-op at Pavol's request, the original kept in the session scratchpad (`stop-hook-git-check.sh.orig`); it returns at each restart of the process, and turning it off again is Pavol's to do in manual mode, since the auto-mode check refuses to schedule it ("The session's automatic permission check refuses a step ..." below). The push loop covers what it protected ("The push loop pushes `main` every 4 minutes ..." below).
- **The Workflow harness runs two agents at once on this box** (four one-command agents in one `parallel()`: agents 0 and 1 started together, agents 2 and 3 after the first pair finished; `batched-climb-plan.md` §2). `model: 'opus'` in `agent()` resolves to a fixed model identifier, readable in each agent transcript's `message.model` field and not written here (the protocol's hard rule that no model identifier is committed); an agent with no `model` inherits the session's. A subagent's floor is about 45k tokens before it does anything (183k for the four). Across agents the prompt cache serves the system prompt and tools, and the first user message only when the whole prompt is identical, because a cache read lands only at a breakpoint the harness placed and a shared prefix inside one message is not one: of the four parallel agents, agents 1–3 read 33,022 tokens (the system prompt and tools) and each wrote its own first message (11,010); of three Workflow agents in one run (`wf_23daeb57-b9f`), the first wrote 62,205 tokens, a second with the identical whole prompt read all 62,205 and wrote none, and a third whose prompt differed only in its last line read 35,434 (the system prompt and tools) and wrote its whole 26,778-token message again. A project agent type (`.claude/agents/<name>.md`) written during the session is not found by `agent({agentType})` ("agent type ... not found") until the session's process restarts, when the registry is read. Such a type's system prompt is shared through the cache: three workflow agents of one project type whose system prompt holds about 40 KB of text (`.claude/agents/cache-probe.md`, untracked; run `wf_e2382567-828`), started one after another within a minute, the first wrote 21,070 tokens, the second and third each read 17,250 and wrote 3,820, their own message; all writes labelled five minutes. So text every agent needs, put in a project type's system prompt, is written once and read by each later agent of the type that starts within the cache's life. A project skill (`.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`) written during the session, unlike an agent type, appears in the session's skill list at once, with no restart (the `fortress-repo`, `remote-container` and `coordinator` skills).
- The VM can be restarted under a live session with the disk intact: worktrees, uncommitted edits and agent transcripts survive; a Workflow run and its agents do not, and the run is resumed with `resumeFromRunId` ("A restart of the session's own process kills its background runs ..." below); the `wip/` branches hold every pushed milestone (`remote-container.md` § The 2026-09-18 restart). A VM restart shows in `uptime -s` and as a `SIGTERM` in the environment manager's log at a run length that is not the cap's ("The platform stops the session's process ..." below), and the kernel build string may change (fc-v33 → fc-v37 once).
- **A user interrupt of the coordinating session's turn kills a background Workflow run**: the rule for every turn is "Stopping a turn kills every background agent alive at that moment" below; the evidence includes a climb batch that lost both its rung agents when an interrupt cut a turn a check-in trigger had started, with no message enqueued and Pavol having pressed nothing he knew of; the `wip/` branches held the rungs' pushed milestones and a worktree its uncommitted report, and the relaunch from the same base continued under the prefix's continuation clause (session `fe616d40`, main transcript and `subagents/`).
- **A message from Pavol that arrives while the coordinator is inside a turn kills a running Workflow's agents, whatever the turn is doing**: this reading is wrong. A message sent during a turn is queued, not an interrupt: it is delivered inside the turn or as the next turn, and every such message during live runs killed none, so the advice at each launch, that messages are safe, is right. The death this reading was made of was an interrupt: both agent transcripts ending at one second with "[Request interrupted by user for tool use]", the journal stopped at their `started` lines, the turn's pending Bash recorded "User rejected tool use", no message enqueued in the window, and the iOS stop button under his right thumb the likely cause (session `fe616d40`, main transcript; `subagents/workflows/wf_eb47c103-304/`).
- **A manual compaction issued between turns leaves a running Workflow alive** (found by a worker in the archived transcript of session `bdff267d`, `transcripts` branch, parts file `001.jsonl`, and confirmed on this session's runs): the eight-rung climb's run survived two `/compact` commands typed between turns, its later rungs' commits and its completion arriving after both boundaries; three manual compactions of this session fell inside live runs, and each run's agents kept writing through the compaction (40 to 66 records inside its window) and went on to their results (session `fe616d40`, `subagents/workflows/`). The rule is the entry below.
- **Stopping a turn kills every background agent alive at that moment; a message sent while the coordinator is busy kills nothing** (`coordinator/interrupt-archaeology/judgement.md` § 1, from `coordinator/interrupt-archaeology/evidence.md`; session `fe616d40`, main transcript, `subagents/` and `subagents/workflows/`; session `bdff267d`, `transcripts` branch, `001.jsonl`). The kill is the turn interrupt the transcript records as "[Request interrupted by user]", with any tool still in flight recorded "User rejected tool use": in the four interrupts that met live background agents all seven agents alive died at that instant, Workflow agents and `Agent`-tool workers alike, and none ever survived one. Eleven messages and three `/context` commands sent while the coordinator was busy, during five live runs, killed nothing: each was queued and delivered inside the running turn or as the next turn. Five manual compactions between turns killed nothing either. That the stop button sent the interrupt is confirmed for one case in Pavol's words and very likely for another (the iOS client's stop control under his right thumb), not shown for a third; the transcripts record the effect, not the control. Not tested: an automatic compaction mid-turn, and an interrupt during the Stop hook while a run is alive. The rule: send messages at any time; compact between turns; do not stop a turn while the session is working, including the seconds after a reply while the transcript backup runs; after an accidental stop, say so and the run is resumed with `resumeFromRunId`, which keeps every agent that had finished (the next entry; POSITIONS, "Check-ins and stops"). An `Agent`-tool worker killed by an interrupt cannot be resumed: a `SendMessage` to it is refused ("was stopped by the user and won't be resumed ... only launch a new agent if the user explicitly asks"), so it is relaunched only at Pavol's explicit ask, the new worker told its predecessor's leftovers (session `fe616d40`, six workers stopped by one interrupt). A Fable worker told to read its predecessor's transcript was ended by the API's safety filter as it printed the transcript's tail (`reasoning_extraction`, the false positive of the `agent()` entry below), so a Fable worker is given the leftovers in the tree and no transcript.
- **A restart of the session's own process kills its background runs, and `resumeFromRunId` then recovers every agent that had finished** (session `fe616d40`; the environment manager's log `/tmp/env-manager.log`). A restart of the session's process (`environment-manager task-run … --session-mode resume`), whether the platform's cap ("The platform stops the session's process ..." below) or a VM restart (the VM entry above), stops every Workflow run, every `Agent`-tool worker and the push loop alive at that moment. The conversation, the session ID, worktrees, untracked files, transcripts and each run's journal survive, and so do shell scripts the workers had started in the background. So the run is resumed, not relaunched: the same script and arguments as at its launch, with `resumeFromRunId`. A finished agent's result is kept, an unfinished one runs from its start, and its worktree's leftovers are its starting point; a relaunch from the base restarts at the first stage instead. An `Agent`-tool worker continues from its transcript on a `SendMessage`. The resume reuses the longest unchanged prefix of the run's `agent()` calls in call order, so it needs the launch's arguments byte for byte and the same order of calls: the base given as a short hash where the launch gave the full hash misses the cache from the first call, and when cached stages resolve at once a pipeline may call its next stage in another order than the live run did and miss from there. A run whose script has changed since launch is resumed from a copy of the script as launched (`git show <base>:<path>`); where the call order would differ, from a copy that forces the live run's order, prompts unchanged, wrapping `agent()` so that the finished calls are issued in the journal's order of their `started` lines (`RESUME_ORDER` and `orderedAgent`; the copies `scratchpad/wf-6.5-run1-resume.js`, `wf-N-run1-resume.js` and `wf-N-run1-land-first-gate.js` in the session's scratchpad are the worked examples). A copy that changes only what follows the cached prefix (a gate skipped, a commit's prompt extended) runs the changed call live and nothing before it. A stage stopped mid-work can leave its work in the tree: a commit stage killed before it had committed leaves its edits in the main tree, uncommitted, and a resume whose commit prompt names them (a changed prompt, so a new key) checks and keeps them and lands the batch; a gather killed mid-work leaves partial staged state, stashed and moved aside before the resume, and the gather runs again live from its start under its key, the journal then holding two `gather` lines under one `launched` line (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-6.5b/RECORD.md`, "A relaunched gather"). The run's journal is `journal.jsonl` in `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>/subagents/workflows/<run>/`: one `launched` line, then a `started` line per agent call (`key`, `agentId`, `label`, `phase`) and a `result` line with the same key and the agent's structured result, none for an agent that returned nothing; a resumed run appends to the same journal, and an agent run live again under a key the journal holds gets a second `started` line (`coordinator/tools/journal-text.py`, which reads it). What does not carry over is a new session: `remote-container.md` § The 2026-09-18 restart and step 5 of the recovery list.
- **The platform stops the session's process after about 12 hours 58 minutes of continuous running, and restarts it in resume mode within seconds** (the environment manager's log `/tmp/env-manager.log`). Every stop in the log is a `SIGTERM` from outside ("Received signal, shutting down gracefully", signal `terminated`), followed by "Claude Code stopped due to context cancellation" with the run's length, then "Set session mode for environment" `resume`. The runs the cap ended are all of nearly the same length, 46,636 to 46,660 s (12 h 57 min 16 s to 12 h 57 min 49 s); the rest are short runs of a few minutes to a few hours that end when the session goes idle, and VM restarts. The cap's stops are not a crash, not memory and not a message; they fall while Pavol is talking because the process runs continuously only while he or a check-in keeps it busy. Any restart, a VM start included, resets the clock, so the next stop is the last start plus 12 h 58 min, and a check-in armed a few minutes after that time resumes what the stop killed; the last start and the next stop are the boot note's.
- **`explorations/experiment/env.sh` is the one script every probe and gate runner sources, and it is verified from its new home** (after `experiment/` moved under `explorations/`): it derives `FORTRESS_HOME` from its own location two levels up, and re-running the two shadow experiments that source it, `reviews/mie-probes/forest/forest-run.sh` (423 s) and `perf-probes/nat/runtime/run-all.sh` (669 s), reproduced every committed count and probe output (`checker-count.txt`'s six counts, stock 103 and forest 37 among them, and captures r1-r5 byte-identical); the only differences were dates, timings and line numbers shifted by later library commits. The separate analysis session's scripts keep their own `experiment/` paths, which name that session's tree.
- **An agent that waits longer than the prompt cache lives writes its whole context again at every wake** (session `fe616d40`, `subagents/agent-af9b2c3ba93eb9c88.jsonl`, probe P1's worker, its usage records deduplicated by message id). Of the 7.0M P1's worker wrote in 263 calls, 6.6M were 19 calls that each wrote 240K to 330K, its whole context, with no cache read, every one after a wait of 8 to 13 minutes on a build or a run; between waits its calls read the cache. The cache's life is in the API's usage records: every cache write of the main session is labelled one hour (`cache_creation.ephemeral_1h_input_tokens`) and every subagent's five minutes (`ephemeral_5m_input_tokens`), as the platform's own description of the main session's wake-ups says of the main session. A poll within the life reads the cache and renews it, so a wait in steps costs a cache read per step. A workflow agent's waits are capped at 270 s for this reason (`wait_for` in `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`); an `Agent`-tool worker's brief carries the same cap, its long run polled in steps under 270 s, or the run handed to a script while the agent ends its turn.
- **A headless `claude -p` session started from the coordinating session's shell keeps its prompt cache for an hour, as the coordinating session does, and an Agent-tool subagent for five minutes** (the usage records: the headless skill writer's first run wrote 19,390 tokens, every one labelled `ephemeral_1h_input_tokens`; the Agent-tool skill writer, woken after a day, wrote 296,876, labelled `ephemeral_5m_input_tokens`, before a one-line fix; resumed about six and a half minutes after its first run, the headless writer read its whole context, 44,900 tokens, from the cache and wrote 109). A headless session takes the coordinating session's id from `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` unless `--session-id` names another, and `--resume <id>` continues it (`explorations/coordinator/tools/skill-writer.sh`). So a worker that waits on the curator between tasks runs as a headless session, resumed within the hour.
- **An agent launched from the coordinating session loads the `fortress-repo` skill on its own, as its first step, when its task touches the repository**: five Agent-tool workers launched from it (a tool edit, an archaeology, an audit, a context study, a run check) each called it first, four of them with no word about it in their briefs (their transcripts, the `Skill` call). `CLAUDE.md` tells every agent to load it before any build, test run, edit, measurement, commit or agent launch; a Workflow agent gets the same `CLAUDE.md`. Not measured: an agent that only reads and reports, which none of those words names.
- **A check-in cadence under an hour is a series of one-shot `send_later` check-ins armed together in one turn, not a cron trigger and not a re-armed one-shot** (a worker's search of session `fe616d40`'s main transcript at Pavol's request). The scheduler's cron triggers take an hour as their shortest interval. Seven `send_later` calls in one turn, each `{"at": ..., "name": "Batch 5 check-in N", "message": ...}` 45 minutes apart, fired within a minute of each target, with no re-arming; a series 90 minutes apart and a chain of one `send_later` per check-in, each re-issued by the turn it started, are the other forms tried. The scheduler refuses more than about ten trigger creations a minute: the eleventh `send_later` of a series got "Trigger creation rate limit reached. Try again in 56s." A series ends when its last check-in has fired, so a run that outlasts it needs a new series, armed by the last check-in. The cadence is 45 minutes (POSITIONS, "Check-ins and stops").
- **`agent()` in a Workflow returns null for an agent the harness marks failed, even after the agent delivered its structured output** (`coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`, "An agent that comes back with nothing"). A second skeptic returned its verdict, an approval with one required correction, through the structured-output tool; the API's safety filter then blocked its next message, a false-positive `reasoning_extraction` refusal, and the harness marked the agent failed (the run's `journal.jsonl`, `"type":"failed"`). `agent()` returned null, and the script recorded the rung as `dropped`, although that approval was committed on the rung's `wip/` branch. Every `agent()` call of the batch script goes through `callAgent`, which treats a null or undefined result and a thrown error alike and runs the role up to two more times, each retry told what the earlier attempt may have left (`ATTEMPTS` and `callAgent` in `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`, the retry's head written by `retryHead` from the stage's `recover…` list).
- **`node --check` does not check the batch script as the Workflow harness parses it, so a spliced script is checked by parsing it as an async function body** (`coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`). Two unescaped apostrophes inside a single-quoted string of `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` once passed `node --check` and were refused by the Workflow parser at launch; the harness runs the script as a function body. On this container's Node, v22.22.2, `node --check` exits 0 on a two-line file holding `export const meta = {}` and the same slip and refuses the slip alone. The check that catches it: the script's text, with `export const meta` made `const meta`, handed to `new AsyncFunction(...)` (`AsyncFunction` being `Object.getPrototypeOf(async function(){}).constructor`), which throws "Unexpected identifier 's'" on the slip and accepts the script without it.
- **The session's automatic permission check refuses a step that lands work on an earlier gate than the one the record names, even after Pavol's go in chat, and his switch to manual approval is the way through** (session `fe616d40`). In auto mode it refused twice to move a gate's earlier outputs (`tmp/gate-batch-N.prev-0653`) back over a later, stopped run's, after Pavol's "Land on the first gate.", and then refused a change to a check-in trigger's prompt that would have done the same, naming it an auto-mode bypass; its rule is that a refused outcome is not pursued by another tool or a later turn. Pavol switched the session to manual approval, the move then ran with no prompt at all, and he switched back to auto after the launch. A `/permissions` allow rule for the command is the other way he has. In manual mode a Workflow agent's commands wait for his approval: a gate judge once waited on one prompt for 29 minutes, the gap in its transcript; auto mode lets a batch run unattended. The check also refused a check-in trigger whose prompt would turn the platform's git-check Stop hook off again after a restart ("Logging/Audit Tampering", the coordinator's log), and that outcome is not pursued (the transcript backup's entry above; `coordinator/remote-container.md` § How the snapshot works).
- **The push loop pushes `main` every 4 minutes when every unpushed commit touches only `explorations/`, and otherwise only the backup branch `wip/main-backup`, so that a container loss loses nothing and `main` stays gated** does not hold: no push loop runs, and the coordinator pushes `main` and `claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8` itself after every commit. The loop's script is `scratchpad/autopush.sh` in the session's scratchpad, its log `scratchpad/autopush.log`; its fallback branch `wip/main-backup`, which took the commits that touched paths outside `explorations/` so that `main` stayed gated, held nothing that `main` does not and is deleted from the remote with the other `wip/` branches but the last batch's rung branches (`coordinator/PLAN.md`, the housekeeping item under "Off the path, parked").

## The ledger

- Rows are never renumbered or moved, and the reports cite them by number; the counts by kind are derived by script in the ledger's counts (`fortress-gap-ledger.md:886`), and the revival worklist (46 items, `fortress-gap-ledger.md:746`) and `apl/lessons.md` are the two derived views. Five cost rows sit in section 15; whether they get a section of their own is Pavol's call.

content.content:
1	<!-- What Pavol has decided, holds or already knows, as it stands now: each position in plain words, what we do and why, under a bold title that is its handle; a quote only where his words are the position itself. Timeless: no dates, no provenance, no account of how a position was reached. That record is `POSITIONS-history.md`, where every earlier text of every entry stands verbatim with what became of it. A position he has replaced is gone from here and the later one stands; a decision not yet built keeps the detail the coming work needs. A worker or a coordinator may add an entry with a date or a quote in it; the next consolidation compiles that out into the history and leaves the position. Standing directives about how we work are in `explorations/protocol.md`, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. Read whole at session start, so that none of it is re-asked or re-explained. -->
2	
3	# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground
4	
5	## The goal
6	
7	- **The measuring stick.** Finish what the designers intended, judged by the specification in `Specification/`, the Working Draft of 2010-12 as the revival revises it, with the 2012 Types chapter cited beside it; not redesign the language. The measure is one program, microGPT, compiled to bytecode and running fast. A pure-Java microGPT is written later as the floor to measure against. The specification is a living document that reflects the changes we make. The tree is tagged `sealed-tree` at the map's last commit; commits after it edit the original sources, test-driven.
8	- **How he weighs his calls where the designers left no word.** "I don't care about type theoretical purity and I'm accepting all unfinished corners of the language because I want to get to a compiled version of micro GPT. And I think this is the right pragmatic approach so that we do not get bogged down in weeds. Theory. We want to get this one program running fast. That's our guiding star. But along the way, I want to stay true to the spirit of Fortress." He has not read the specification, the papers on its type system or the library, and relies on the record: "I assume those people knew much more than I do right now." The check he asked for is a thorough top-tier review of every decision of his against the designers' intent, for errors of commission and of omission (`reviews/decisions-review/evidence.md`, `judgement.md`, `popl-recheck.md`); its items are decisions below.
9	- **The readable expression.** The toy problem is microGPT and the search is for its most readable expression: "we are searching for the optimal expression of the microGPT algorithm for readability." Fortress's mathematical notation and Iverson's APL notation (with Hsu's data design for data-flow algorithms) are the two sources. The Hsu-style flat program gave "a few lumps of coal", not a diamond; the vocabulary is where any polishing happens. C4 is the APL target form; C2's tuple hyperparameter form is what a strand assignment expands to; the semicolon form is set aside.
10	- **The APL side quest is closed.** It was a curiosity, then a ladder to learn APL, then native code (not an interpreter in an interpreter) with microGPT as its target; its remaining ground (tacit, characters, nested arrays) is not pursued.
11	- **The 2D notation is a gimmick.** Fortify's mathematical rendering is "a neat gimmick, not a good idea": it encodes one perspective on a computation into the syntax, while the same mathematics can be written many ways; APL's glyph-per-transformation is the purer realisation. Presentation only, not on the path, not an argument for Fortress; no work on it unless he asks.
12	- **The type checker on interpreter programs.** He wants the checker, which runs only on the compile path, usable on interpreter programs, and considers it low-hanging fruit. It comes after the switch-over, when walk also takes the static coercions the checker inserts (the entry on walk's choice of coercions).
13	
14	## History he knows (do not re-explain)
15	
16	- **The project's end.** DARPA's HPCS did not take Sun into phase three (2006) and the project lived on at Sun Labs until 2012. His reading: they did no work on performance, "mucked around with syntax", and the promise that a sufficiently advanced compiler would later make mathematical types fast was never true; the funding was pulled for good reason.
17	- **Boxed numerics.** The compiled path is only about ten times the interpreter because numerics are boxed (`FRR64`, no `DADD`); "without unboxed doubles and arrays of doubles, what are we even doing here". The first measurement's scalar loop was an edge case microGPT never hits (literals in the loop, a `:=` accumulator); the fairer test he asked for agreed with him (FACTS § Execution model). The storage is his decision below; unboxed arithmetic is phase 6 of the plan.
18	- **Hsu's critique** of language paradigms as accidental complexity; he is "coming around to his point of view".
19	- **The third-party Java 9 port** gets no credit and no mention: "I don't wanna see them mentioned anywhere." CLAUDE.md no longer describes the tree as the port's migration grafted on the history; the other files that repeat that sentence wait for the lineage cleanup (`PLAN.md`). His plan to rename the graft-free `clean-ladder` branch to `main` was not carried out.
20	
21	## Decisions on record
22	
23	### The standard and the sources
24	
25	- **The specification stays the standard, the Types chapter beside it.** Where the Types chapter of the team's unfinished restart (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`) covers a topic, it is cited beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word: the exclusion rule as "instantiation exclusion" in its two-part form, the `covariant` modifier, `Bottom` inexpressible. "On the rule S revises, it is the designers' latest intent, and the goal is to finish what they intended."
26	- **The type group's late positions outweigh the early text.** The specification "was written in a vacuum early on", "as a wish"; "then the type group went in and tried to make it run. So they knew much more about what's feasible and what's not. The goal was performance. The specialization is a must"; "when that wish met reality, then the spec must change"; "whatever the spec was dreaming about in 2008 is irrelevant because it met hard reality". So the late, implementation-informed positions of the type group (the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the compiled tower flattened by Steele in 2011, Naden's 2012 write-up, the POPL 2019 paper) outweigh the specification's earlier text where they conflict, and the implementers' later word outweighs unfinished text. "We are not Naden. We know nothing here."
27	- **The library's own practice is the standard.** "all the extensions that [microGPT] invented need to go directly to the standard library in the spirit of the standard library." Exclusion "is a practice that is all over the standard library"; whoever extends the library "should study the existing parts of the Fortress library meticulously, and use those patterns for extending the standard library in the native way". 85	- **Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason.** "our plan needs to update the spec with the change that we do and somehow properly record why we decided that way, so that there is no open discrepancy between the spec and our implementation that would be confusing to people. We need to preserve the original historic record somewhere in a document with our reasoning why we did the switch and preserve the option to go the route C." Every change takes the S1 form, an original-tree edit flagged as such; `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is never touched.
86	- **The S1 form**, the layered form the team used for 1.0 and its 2009 draft: a labelled callout at each changed passage that prints in every build (not a `\note`); a revival section in Appendix I (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), each entry with the reason, the original sentences quoted with their path and line in the unrevised copy, and route C with what reversing to it would take; one paragraph in the front matter; the full reasoning in a repository document. The unrevised copy is called "the Working Draft of February 2011", in the team's own form, each citation giving the path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; Appendix I says once that the directory's name is misleading, since only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Appendix I's introduction says that the entries follow the revival's decisions, route A the first of them, each naming its own.
87	- **The refused examples (S2).** Each example the exclusion rule refuses is revised to the one library's shape, the original kept in the text as "Not allowed", the specification's own form, and the rule stated once in Luchangco's two-part form under "instantiation exclusion". Built. The `covariant` keyword gets one sentence in the revival callout at the covariance example, saying that the type group's later design declares variance with a `covariant` modifier, implemented on neither path, and pointing to the decision record and row 404. The number chapters (`basic-lib/basic-integers.tex`, `basic-lib/numbers.tex`, `advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex`) changed in the same batch as the flattening, never earlier. The calculi of Appendix A (Core Fortress with Where Clauses, ACFFD and Basic Core) each carry a `\revision` callout saying that the calculus predates instantiation exclusion and admits the shapes the rule refuses, their rules and soundness claims untouched. The judgement's candidate ledger rows 2, 3 and 5 are parked (`PLAN.md`).
88	- **Appendix I's small items.** `TotalComparison` extends `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]` in the api and the component, its five restated members kept, so that it gets back `MIN` and `MAX` (row 461 closed; built; taken on the coordinator's recommendation, and he wants it explained in more detail when he has the energy, "I need to pay that down", so it is on the list for his review).
89	
90	### How we work
91	
92	- **Test first, the test kept.** Every sealed-tree edit starts from a failing test added to the corpus: the worker writes the test first, verifies that it actually fails, makes the fix, proves it passes, and the test stays in the corpus from then on; the full suite stays green. The unacceptable process is the one-off validation script, proving once by hand that the interpreter and the compiler agree and leaving no permanent check. The batches fix the issues the explorations captured as ledger rows, each with how to reproduce it, "Those are like our bug reports": the worker first commits the reproduction into the test suite, "this is how I have reproduced what the previous probe has discovered", then makes the fix, and the test passing demonstrates that the issue is fixed; "There isn't much more to it." The test captures the essence of the problem, not the shape the probe met it in, "do not blindly transpose the issue from the probe like think about it what's the core problem and capture that", written as a clean minimal version. Whether the test was seen failing first is read from the worker's transcript, not shown by a committed capture. The skeptic checks it there and runs no build to repeat it: "It should just check that the procedure of test first was followed. Not that it should be repeating the whole process, that is a fucking waste." Whether the suite runs per edit or per landed batch is an engineering choice, and per batch is in line with the rule. Every measured and repaired defect gets a gated assertion, a deferred spec-settled one an `XXX` test. The test needs no commit of its own: the order is test written, seen failing through the harness, the fix, the test seen passing, and the test and the fix may land in one commit ("I don't recall asking for test and fix to be separated into different commits ... I would worry about increasing the ceremony burden").
93	- **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test passes or fails, as the team designed the suite, and a value that matters is asserted in the test with the mechanisms the suite already has (an `assert` in an interpreter test, `run_out_equals` in a compiled one): "what is the purpose of a test suit that you just cannot run it and get a green? If everything that's encoded in it is, is okay and it turns red if it's not, why would you have to compare some values that it outputs? Those values must be part of the test." What a test prints beyond its checks does not matter: "When the designers of the test suite decided that it passes without any additional check, it is not needed to control its outputs." So no batch compares the corpus's printed outputs, no baseline is run to compare against, and no expected-output files are added to the interpreter suite, which has none; none of it is offered to him again.
94	- **Nothing is built or run twice on the same code.** "We don't want to re be rebuilding stuff that doesn't need to be rebuilt." The design, agreed with him and built into the batch script: the old code, the batch's base, is built once per batch, by the coordinator, before the launch, in a worktree nobody compiles or runs in (the script's `args.baseBuild`); "We just mechanically take the latest build and share it between each rung from the same baseline": every rung worktree is seeded from that one build in seconds (`coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`), never built clean (his "Duh!" to "seeding a worktree by copying a built tree rather than rebuilding it"); the worker builds only what its own edit changed; the skeptic builds nothing, "very smart skeptics that just like reuse everything that was built during the rank phase as much as possible and just do their independent checks": it reads test-first from the worker's transcript, runs its own small programs on the new code with the rung's build and on the old code against the batch's one base build, through the rung's private seeded copy of it so that no two agents compile into one cache; the second skeptic checks only the repair against its own refusal; no stage re-runs a build, a suite or a measurement on a code state another stage has already run, and no agent reads again a log of output that has not changed: "I want to eliminate all waste of this type. Where we are re-executing stuff for no reason." How a worktree is seeded and what a worker clears after an edit or a failed build is engineering, measured before it is built into the batch script (`coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md`; the blinded engineers' variants in `coordinator/process-engineering/cache-sharing.md`).
95	- **The coordinator watches what it launches.** Only a long or large run the coordinator launches outside a batch, a probe that builds and runs suites for an hour or more, is watched against the estimate it was launched with, so that none runs away as probe P1 did (`coordinator/process-engineering/p1-cost.md`); when it passes its estimate the coordinator reacts, by an instruction to the worker or a stop, and its brief carries what keeps it efficient, a wait polled under the prompt cache's life among it. Ordinary workers carry no such procedure, and no ask is added before a probe: "I don't want you to become paranoid about running probes"; "I don't want the cargo cult of ... monitoring here. Only longer runs. ... I don't want you to burden with ... procedure on each call to workers." P1's waste was one the worker knew how to avoid: "an instruction to that worker would have corrected it." Watching the spend is the coordinator's, never the worker's: a brief does not ask a worker to measure, project or cap its own token spend, "it has its job. It is not its job to monitor the token spend. It's yours."; the coordinator reads the spend from the agents' transcripts (`explorations/coordinator/tools/spend.py`).
96	- **A deeper pass, not a halt.** When something goes wrong or turns out undecided, the answer is a deeper pass, not a halt or a rollback. On a red gate over a merged batch, no bisection of commits: "we should identify the source of the conflict holistically and rework that part in the merged batch", because the goal is one tree with everything running rather than the largest subset that happens to be green. On a divergence the specification does not settle, no stop: "it is not a reason to stop the climb, it is the reason to think harder, review the architecture and holistically decide on the best path forward and execute that one." What reaches him are the forks already reserved in `PLAN.md`, not new ones invented at the point of difficulty.
97	- **Forks are probed before a batch is briefed.** "if there are known decision forks, which we can evaluate using probes, we should be doing these during this phase, during this planning phase": a fork a probe can settle is probed first, so that the decision is his and the worker gets a clean task, never a decision left to a worker and reviewed after the fact. Rows are taken one per message with refreshers (other languages, what makes sense in a high-performance language), not in groups.
98	- **A brief describes the problem, not the solution.** "How do we prevent the myopic view? … I want to have full creativity of solutions": a worker that has not read our notes lists every way the language and the library offer before a design choice reaches him; a rule that blocks an option is answered with how the library gets around it (protocol principle 2). A worker that records timings records the CPU too, so that comparisons can be guessed at.
99	- **The mission briefing.** "this whole exercise is about in-context learning. You were not pre-trained on Fortress. And the language was not finished." The planner, who has the whole map, gives each rung a mission briefing from the map that its agents read in their first turn; the share of agents that use it is reported with each landing (it was about 80% once and fell to 25-35%: "We need to get back to that level"). The briefing is in neutral words, "the decisions on record" ("I am trying to stay humble and I don't want to see my name in there multiple times. Make this neutral."); the worker answers no required questions about its search ("I disagree with the procedural enforcement here ... it's giving the agent side quests that it's graded on instead of something that it should just take into consideration during the implementation"; the briefing says "this is not a Java, this is not a Scala, you are in unfamiliar territory", and then the worker "should focus on its tasks"); the skeptic checks the result against the library's way, the ledger and sibling sites, and the decisions on record.
100	- **No re-measuring what the record holds.** "you are wasting resources on remeasuring." A brief hands over what the record has measured as findings to cite and names the one new thing to measure; a clean worker is clean of our options, not of our measurements (protocol principle 5). A rung whose test is the checker-count or distance stage takes the last landed gate's tables as its before and does not re-run the stage on an unchanged base; the gate commits its per-site list so that the before is complete. The nine steps are a way to brief him on unfamiliar ground, a type-theoretical question answered from the theory, the rule and a few declarations; and one global rule is sought from type theory and the peers' implementations rather than a rule slapped on a rule ("I cannot be trusted to derive a rule that wouldn't break the whole system and be a hodgepodge of edge cases").
101	- **Reversible stops do not hold a batch.** A stop a batch record reserves for him (a model or APL line beyond the approved ones, an interpreter output a rung cannot account for): "These don't need me now. They are reversible things I can review later. Don't block start of next batches on these." It lands, the push and the next batch go ahead, and it is listed for his review (the protocol's first hard rule). An output difference the untouched tree already shows from run to run, the test's verdict unchanged, is not a stop but a ledger row ("we had a rule too stringent because the spirit of the test is still held"); a rung's small items go to the ledger for review, not to him one per message.
102	- **Which decisions taken inside the work reach Pavol, and how.** A decision an agent takes is consequential when it reverses a decision on record, bends it or reads it anew; changes a line of the model program; touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation; chooses among ways the record does not settle; or cannot be undone. Everything else an agent decided is listed for later review, a rung's small items in the ledger, and holds nothing up. A consequential decision reaches Pavol one of three ways: asked before the work, a fork known in advance probed and put in the ask form before the batch is briefed; landed, then reviewed, one that can be undone landing, named in one line at the landing, listed in PLAN under the batch's list with the default that landed and put to Pavol later, one per message; or a stop that holds the work, one that cannot be undone or would act against Pavol's word, put at once. The `coordinator` skill states it (`decisions.md`, "Decisions and how they reach the curator").
103	- **A blocking second review does not hold a green batch.** "we have enough rigor or robustness and backup in our processes after that, so that small failure in a rule should not be blocking ... landing large ships like this." After its one repair round, a merged-diff review that still blocks does not hold a batch whose gate is green: the batch lands, the review's remaining findings go to the next batch and are listed for his review, and the post-batch review follows. A red gate after its repair still stops a batch. Built into `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` and its manual. The merged-diff review itself stays inside the batch, once, beside the gate, as the check of the merged tree's records, the stops and the routing before the push; removing it and moving its checks to the review after the batch is not taken (Fable's review of the batch practice against the Opus review's; he sided with Fable).
104	- **A tests-only repair does not rerun the gate.** "we are being overly pedantic for no good reason with like how the gates are set up ... we have to be weighing costs and benefits and we are not skipping the test, we are adding the test, we are moving stuff to following batches, we are running reviews after the fact, so we will catch stuff that the rerunning of a gate is not." A repair after the gate reruns the gate only when it changes something the gate reads: the code under `ProjectFortress/` other than test files, the library under `Library/`, or `build.xml`. Any other repair (new tests, the specification's text, the records) runs its new tests in the harness on the merged tree; the first gate's tables stand; the landing records the new tests beside them. The same weighing of cost against what a rule protects applies to every rule of the batch workflow. Built.
105	- **What a batch commits.** "the commit discipline in a branch should not be different from what you will be committing to the main. Like don't keep temporary shit around. We are backing up the transcripts anyway from all the workers. So if we need to dig up something, how the worker arrived at some point, we have the full transcripts." A worker commits, on its own branch as on `main`, only what `main` is to hold: the Fortress change, its tests, its report, the lines for the ledger, FACTS and the plan, and a script or tool that is reusable ("If that script that batch contributes a script that is reusable, it goes in there", such as the documented way of running the checker as a shadow); no captured outputs, logs, raw outputs, script copies or other scratch are committed anywhere; new issues go to the ledger, reports into the batch's report; the process, and whether a worker wrote its test first and saw it fail, is read from the workers' transcripts, which the backup keeps. Deleting the `wip/` branches after a gate is his own chore in the GitHub web page, and he is not reminded of it. Built into the script, its manual and the protocol.
106	- **Workers commit their own files as they go.** "Workers should be committing themselves as they go, focused their files only. Protects against container failures and stops from harness bothering you about uncommitted files." They push to their own `wip/` branches as they work; the wip branches are cleaned up after the gate; the workflow script lives in the repository, not only in a session; the coordinator pushes `main` every few minutes ("I hope we are committing as we go because I worry that the container will get reset"). A protocol hard rule.
107	- **Which tier runs what.** "You can spend as much Opus workers as you want." The highest-risk decisions touch all three of specification, interpreter and compiler, which may disagree, and the design intent has to be inferred from the breadcrumbs left in all of them; the cheaper tier gathers the evidence into a condensed brief, and the high-level judgement of what makes sense given all the signals and what design balance lets the project grow belongs to the top tier, because that is the work it is for. Workers are pinned to Opus by the alias, "to make that workflow future proof"; the expensive model is escalated only at decision points, "sparsely so that it doesn't have to gather all the context by running multiple tool calls". Sonnet is the tier for archaeology. Two workers launched on the wrong tier once cost him 1.7 million tokens "down the drain". The coordinating session runs on Opus, so that Fable's own weekly pool is kept "for more important work"; it moves to Fable at his word when the pool on all models is spent, and how the Opus trial is judged is in `coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-27-record-keeping.md`.
108	- **The judge's rulings.** A judge's first ruling on a rung or on the merged tree runs on Opus; a second ruling on the same rung or tree runs on Fable ("Second ruling is for Fable."), named in `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` (`judgeTier`), so Fable is spent only when a second ruling happens. The review's judge rules while the gate runs on, and the gate writes its outputs under `tmp/` until the commit stage. A second repair round is not taken; option (b), approvals with required corrections when the fix is already written, has not been put to him (parked, `PLAN.md`).
109	- **The Fable rule.** "whenever it touches those three aspects of uh, library specification and implementation we are running the fable so if you use it sparingly I can pre-approve every such decision." The coordinator runs a Fable judgement without asking, sparingly, for a design question that touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation, once an Opus worker's evidence or list of ways is on file and the record has been searched and does not already settle it; he learns of it when the judgement is put to him in the ask form. <!-- What Pavol has decided, holds or already knows, as it stands now: each position in plain words, what we do and why, under a bold title that is its handle; a quote only where his words are the position itself. Timeless: no dates, no provenance, no account of how a position was reached. That record is `POSITIONS-history.md`, where every earlier text of every entry stands verbatim with what became of it. A position he has replaced is gone from here and the later one stands; a decision not yet built keeps the detail the coming work needs. A worker or a coordinator may add an entry with a date or a quote in it; the next consolidation compiles that out into the history and leaves the position. Standing directives about how we work are in `explorations/protocol.md`, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. Read whole at session start, so that none of it is re-asked or re-explained. -->

# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground

## The goal

- **The measuring stick.** Finish what the designers intended, judged by the specification in `Specification/`, the Working Draft of 2010-12 as the revival revises it, with the 2012 Types chapter cited beside it; not redesign the language. The measure is one program, microGPT, compiled to bytecode and running fast. A pure-Java microGPT is written later as the floor to measure against. The specification is a living document that reflects the changes we make. The tree is tagged `sealed-tree` at the map's last commit; commits after it edit the original sources, test-driven.
- **How he weighs his calls where the designers left no word.** "I don't care about type theoretical purity and I'm accepting all unfinished corners of the language because I want to get to a compiled version of micro GPT. And I think this is the right pragmatic approach so that we do not get bogged down in weeds. Theory. We want to get this one program running fast. That's our guiding star. But along the way, I want to stay true to the spirit of Fortress." He has not read the specification, the papers on its type system or the library, and relies on the record: "I assume those people knew much more than I do right now." The check he asked for is a thorough top-tier review of every decision of his against the designers' intent, for errors of commission and of omission (`reviews/decisions-review/evidence.md`, `judgement.md`, `popl-recheck.md`); its items are decisions below.
- **The readable expression.** The toy problem is microGPT and the search is for its most readable expression: "we are searching for the optimal expression of the microGPT algorithm for readability." Fortress's mathematical notation and Iverson's APL notation (with Hsu's data design for data-flow algorithms) are the two sources. The Hsu-style flat program gave "a few lumps of coal", not a diamond; the vocabulary is where any polishing happens. C4 is the APL target form; C2's tuple hyperparameter form is what a strand assignment expands to; the semicolon form is set aside.
- **The APL side quest is closed.** It was a curiosity, then a ladder to learn APL, then native code (not an interpreter in an interpreter) with microGPT as its target; its remaining ground (tacit, characters, nested arrays) is not pursued.
- **The 2D notation is a gimmick.** Fortify's mathematical rendering is "a neat gimmick, not a good idea": it encodes one perspective on a computation into the syntax, while the same mathematics can be written many ways; APL's glyph-per-transformation is the purer realisation. Presentation only, not on the path, not an argument for Fortress; no work on it unless he asks.
- **The type checker on interpreter programs.** He wants the checker, which runs only on the compile path, usable on interpreter programs, and considers it low-hanging fruit. It comes after the switch-over, when walk also takes the static coercions the checker inserts (the entry on walk's choice of coercions).

## History he knows (do not re-explain)

- **The project's end.** DARPA's HPCS did not take Sun into phase three (2006) and the project lived on at Sun Labs until 2012. His reading: they did no work on performance, "mucked around with syntax", and the promise that a sufficiently advanced compiler would later make mathematical types fast was never true; the funding was pulled for good reason.
- **Boxed numerics.** The compiled path is only about ten times the interpreter because numerics are boxed (`FRR64`, no `DADD`); "without unboxed doubles and arrays of doubles, what are we even doing here". The first measurement's scalar loop was an edge case microGPT never hits (literals in the loop, a `:=` accumulator); the fairer test he asked for agreed with him (FACTS § Execution model). The storage is his decision below; unboxed arithmetic is phase 6 of the plan.
- **Hsu's critique** of language paradigms as accidental complexity; he is "coming around to his point of view".
- **The third-party Java 9 port** gets no credit and no mention: "I don't wanna see them mentioned anywhere." CLAUDE.md no longer describes the tree as the port's migration grafted on the history; the other files that repeat that sentence wait for the lineage cleanup (`PLAN.md`). His plan to rename the graft-free `clean-ladder` branch to `main` was not carried out.

## Decisions on record

### The standard and the sources

- **The specification stays the standard, the Types chapter beside it.** Where the Types chapter of the team's unfinished restart (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`) covers a topic, it is cited beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word: the exclusion rule as "instantiation exclusion" in its two-part form, the `covariant` modifier, `Bottom` inexpressible. "On the rule S revises, it is the designers' latest intent, and the goal is to finish what they intended."
- **The type group's late positions outweigh the early text.** The specification "was written in a vacuum early on", "as a wish"; "then the type group went in and tried to make it run. So they knew much more about what's feasible and what's not. The goal was performance. The specialization is a must"; "when that wish met reality, then the spec must change"; "whatever the spec was dreaming about in 2008 is irrelevant because it met hard reality". So the late, implementation-informed positions of the type group (the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the compiled tower flattened by Steele in 2011, Naden's 2012 write-up, the POPL 2019 paper) outweigh the specification's earlier text where they conflict, and the implementers' later word outweighs unfinished text. "We are not Naden. We know nothing here."
- **The library's own practice is the standard.** "all the extensions that [microGPT] invented need to go directly to the standard library in the spirit of the standard library." Exclusion "is a practice that is all over the standard library"; whoever extends the library "should study the existing parts of the Fortress library meticulously, and use those patterns for extending the standard library in the native way". No fix is designed from a reading of the specification alone or from a user-side workaround. A fork put to him names the library's own way first, and a fork resting on a rule that refuses something says what the library does instead (protocol principle 2). The lesson behind the rule: he had to find the diagonal's override shape himself ("why the fuck did I have to invent this solution?"), because the step skipped was what the library already does in the same family.
- **Fleshing out the standard library** is a very important task: first the `RR64`/`AdditiveGroup` mismatch (done by the flattening), then the algebraic layer (Ring, Field and what ML's matrices and tensors need) so the library's trait flavour reaches them; into the standard library itself, not a tree of our own.
- **Interpreter performance is irrelevant.** "interpreter of Fortress, which is hundreds times slower than the Python interpreter, is irrelevant for any performance discussions"; "we cannot judge anything performance related in Fortress while we do not have a compiler". No edit to C4 for speed, and no performance decision of any kind until microGPT runs compiled. The two microGPT programs never run in the gate ("those are too long running to be tests"); the ladder-regression stage compiles them and records the phase; when they one day run, the run goes to a separate non-gating stage.
- **Development-loop performance is a first-class concern.** When an iteration waits too long on something, find the cause and fix it.
- **The territory map** (`coordinator/map/`) is the map down to where the design intent is written, papers as well as the specification; he wanted it before unsealing. The maps exist so that nothing on record is rediscovered; the boot order is followed as written, `INDEX.md` included.
- **The plan** (`coordinator/PLAN.md`) is six phases, approved with its workers: 1, the wrapping operators, the specification rung without the number chapters and the run-time size rung; 2, the flattening, the number chapters and the overflow natives; 3, the checker at a true zero; 4, the switch-over, natives then names; 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code-generation holes; 6, microGPT fast. Phases 1 and 2 are landed. His answers come in the plan's order; the re-approval rows and the other off-path items are parked until relevant; row 41 joins the switch-over's design.

### The one library and the compiled checker

- **The library route.** "we need to unify this. into single library"; "the compiler second library is just a bootstrap and we need to get rid of it." One library, the interpreter's (`FortressLibrary` + `FortressBuiltin`), becomes the library the compiler checks; no declaration goes into the compiler's prelude (`CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra`); the prelude-name rungs of the ladder stopped, code-generator rungs continue; the three prelude files are deleted at the switch-over and their tests kept. How the checker is brought to accept the library is a plan put to him step by step, not a decision to re-ask.
- **The compiler prelude's leftovers go at the switch-over.** The compiler-prelude block for `Maybe` stands as landed, its tests kept, its lines gone then; the guard `if other = -1 then 0` in the two compiled `REM` bodies (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:601`, `:686`) stays and goes with the prelude; the prelude's reversed spellings of the wrapping and saturating operators (row 348) are respelled then, in 10 compiled test files; `ZZ64`'s compiled shift declaration (row 381) closes when the compiled path reads this library; the specification's `shift` (row 383) reaches the compiled path then, `compiler_tests/XXXShiftDeclRungI.test` promoted and `shift` a reserved name on the compiled path from then on, the switch-over batch measuring which compiler tests bind it.
- **The checker count is measured, never red.** The checker-count stage stays in every gate, reported and never red on its own; the full distance measurement (all apis and components) is a report-only stage of the phase-3 gates, whose job is driving it down.
- **Sizes.** The checker checks `nat` and `int` parameters (built). A size left unknown after inference is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value, and nothing otherwise ("the middle is a clear winner"); how the checker represents an unknown size was not his to decide. Deleting the dead sizes (E3, 25 api declarations) is shown to him as a diff with the switch-over's design, with row 41. Every static argument counts in the exclusion rule except operator arguments ("sizes count"); booleans follow once the checker supports boolean parameters (row 406). A size the call cannot fix is an error at that call, also inside overload sets: when the arm the rules would pick has a size the call cannot fix, the call is refused with the same "could not infer" error instead of the arm being dropped (row 400 closed). A `nat` parameter is an `NN32` value and an `int` parameter a `ZZ32` (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:82-90`); a larger one is refused; the array design refuses a JVM array length over 2^31-1 where it makes storage ("that's not even a question"). A size used as a value converts to `ZZ32` as a numeral does (row 485); sizes as `NN32` and ranges as `ZZ32` are consistent, since array lengths and indices are Java `int`, a size is never negative and ranges count through negatives. All built.
- **The run-time size design is B.** A size at run time gets the same descriptor object a type argument has, filling the slot the team's code generator reserved ("of course, let's extend the runtime object with a new field for the size"); one descriptor per number from a table, no holder class, the team's instantiation pattern applied to numbers. Operators are not unified with the descriptor-bearing kinds ("I don't see a need"). Built.
- **The implicit bound of an unbounded type parameter is `Any`**, the top, holding tuples, functions and `()`, which `Object` does not; the library's generic containers are instantiated at tuples, arrays indexed by pairs among them.
